## Why This Topic Matters

Randomization protects treatment comparisons from systematic allocation bias, while blinding reduces differential behavior and assessment.

## Learning Objectives

After working through this material, you should be able to:

- explain the main ideas behind **Randomization of assignment**;
- interpret the R workflow and its output; and
- adapt the examples to a related analysis.

## Lesson Roadmap

The original material is organized around the following topics:

1. Equally sized groups
2. Concealment of Assignments

#### Equally sized groups

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This subsection explains **Equally sized groups** and shows how it contributes to the overall Randomization of assignment workflow.


For normal populations with equal variances, the likelihood
ratio test is most powerful if the sizes of the compared groups are equal.

$$
0>\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{v}}-\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{v_{N / 2}}}=\Phi^{-1}\left(\beta_{N / 2}\right)-\Phi^{-1}(\beta)
$$
where $v_{N / 2}<v$ yields. 

Hence,

$$
\Phi^{-1}(\beta)>\Phi^{-1}\left(\beta_{N / 2}\right) \quad \text { or } \quad \beta>\beta_{N / 2} \quad \text { or } \quad 1- \beta< 1- \beta_{N / 2}
$$

#### Concealment of Assignments

<!-- generated-learning-note -->
This subsection explains **Concealment of Assignments** and shows how it contributes to the overall Randomization of assignment workflow.


The most common randomization are the simple, block, and stratified procedures.

An actual group assignment should be kept secret from the subject as well as
from the physician responsible for administering therapy, if the trial is double blinded. 
when a new subject enters the trial, the physician
should call the central location where the next envelope in the sequence is
opened to reveal the group assignment for the subject.
